subtopic: CANADIAN OBSERVERS IN VIET NAM

speechtext: Will the Canadian observers on duty in Viet Nam have the right to inspect prisons in South Viet Nam and to report on the living conditions of political prisoners?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN OBSERVERS IN VIET NAM
speechtext:
The answer to this question cannot be given in
March 7, 1973

categorical terms. While there is no direct supervisory role to be undertaken by the International Commission in respect of the treatment given to civilian internees, the International Commission of Control and Supervision may become involved in visiting prisons and other places of detention in South Viet Nam. Primary responsibility for carrying out Articles 8 and 9 of the Protocol on Prisoners of the Paris Agreement rests with the two South Vietnamese parties, the Republic of Viet Nam and the Viet Cong. These two parties have agreed to resolve the question of civilian internees between themselves. The basis of this agreement is the 1954 Viet Nam Ceasefire Agreement which formulated a definition of "civilian internees." In the Protocol on Prisoners, the two South Vietnamese parties agree to do their utmost to resolve this question within 90 days of the ceasefire. The observer teams of the International Commission of Control and Supervision are responsible for observing the return of detained civilians in South Viet Nam. This involves sending observer teams to the "last detention places from which these persons will be taken to the places of return" and to "each place in Viet Nam where these persons are being returned." However, the ability to carry out this supervisory function depends on the prior agreement of the two South Vietnamese parties regarding the location and operation of the ICCS teams, and other necessary arrangements to facilitate the operation of the teams. At present, the International Commission of Control and Supervision has made preliminary arrangements to form teams to carry out this supervisory function and is awaiting the required decisions by the South Vietnamese parties. Therefore, the ability of the International Commission of Control and Supervision to discharge its responsibilities concerning prisoners cannot be separated from the matter of the responsibilities of the South Vietnamese parties on this question and their co-operation in laying the groundwork for the release and return of prisoners.

speechtext: In response to the recent press reports concerning drug products on the Canadian market, and my previous question, is the Minister of National Health and Welfare now in a position to assure the House that the Health Protection Branch adequately fulfils its responsibility in assessing the quality of drugs on the Canadian market?

speakeroldname: Mr. Norman A. Cafik (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: SUPPLY AND SERVICES-CONTRACT FOR FILE FOLDERS
subtopic: ASSESSMENT OF DRUG QUALITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the Food and Drugs Act and regulations, all drug manufacturing and distributing facilities, large or small, are inspected by staff of the Health Protection Branch. Detailed and exhaustive examinations are made of the manufacturing process, the facilities and quality control procedures including storage and record-keeping systems and the source of raw materials. This testing may be done by the firm itself or by a competent analytical laboratory.
Newspaper articles alleged that four small Montreal companies were marketing drugs after only minimal testing. Recent inspections which took place before these articles appeared showed that the products sold by these four companies were subjected to a satisfactory level of testing, including appropriate methods for the identity, purity and potency of the product, disintegration of the tablet and, where applicable, expiry date and stability.
The four firms mentioned are only distributors and neither manufacture, label nor package drugs. Their operations involve storage of packaged drugs and distribution only. They maintain the records required by law. Their products are manufactured, packaged and labelled for them by pharmaceutical manufacturers who comply with the requirements of the Food and Drugs Act regulations. Firms such as the forementioned are expected to ensure
Order Paper Questions
that their storage and distribution facilities are acceptable, and these four companies have been so inspected and found satisfactory. It was alleged that the Health Protection Branch did not know of the existence of some of the products of these four companies. This is untrue. These companies and all their products are well known to the Health Protection Branch. The newspapers' claim that Laboratoires Anger Ltee produces ten products is not substantiated either by company records or our own, which list seven.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Before today's proceedings 61 notices of motions for the production of papers had been transferred for debate, to which we must add those that have been transferred today. The great bulk of those motions were transferred for debate at the insistence or the request of the govern-
Motions for Papers
ment on the stated ground that the information or papers sought to be produced were confidential, or some such similar designation. A number of instances have arisen in the past when the government refused to produce documents on the basis that they were confidential and subsequently they became public, thereby proving they were not in fact confidential.
I submit what is happening here is that the government is misusing its authority to transfer items for debate. There are 61 on the order paper now, so many of them will never come up for debate, let alone a vote. I think it is an abuse of the rules of the House to permit the government to hide behind this kind of sham answer of confidentiality.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might comment on the very important point of order raised by the hon. member with regard to the question of notices of motions for the production of papers. I have been very conscious of the very large number of such motions that have appeared on the order paper both in the last and the present parliaments. I have also examined as well as I could the grounds upon which the government has been obligated from time to time to refuse the production of various papers. It places the parliamentary secretary in an unenviable position to have the job each Wednesday of refusing what to hon. members appear to be legitimate requests for information.
The government has reviewed the grounds very carefully, based upon parliamentary practice and based on its willingness to make available as much information as possible to hon. members. I hope that at an early date, when we are debating one of these motions that have been transferred for debate, it will be possible for me to discuss in some detail the grounds upon which we are reaching these decisions and also to table for the benefit of hon. members the guidelines that are being used. It seems to me that if these guidelines, which we think are based upon good practice, are fully understood by hon. members, maybe there will be a better understanding of this question on the part of private members and the government. I would like to have it debated on an appropriate occasion when we are dealing with one of these motions and put before the House, the guidelines that we have brought up to date and are following and are asking departments to follow. The fundamental principle we have adopted is to make as much information as possible available. Only where the refusal can be founded on solid grounds is the request refused.
I make these comments because I believe it is important to indicate that we have considered the matter and are willing at a later date to debate the whole question of notices of motions for papers.

subtopic: COMMITTEE REVIEW OF AND REPORT ON STANDING ORDERS AND PROCEDURE-AUTHORIZATION TO TRAVEL OUTSIDE OF CANADA DURING STUDY

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (President of the Privy Council) moved:
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: COMMITTEE REVIEW OF AND REPORT ON STANDING ORDERS AND PROCEDURE-AUTHORIZATION TO TRAVEL OUTSIDE OF CANADA DURING STUDY
speechtext:
Standing Orders and Procedure
That the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization be authorized to consider the standing orders of the House and procedure in both the House and its committees with special regard to all the matters that Mr. Speaker suggested during the twenty-eighth and twenty-ninth parliaments that may require the consideration of the said committee, and to report to the House its views on any facets thereof that may require reform and to recommend what manner of reform may be required;
And that the committee be authorized to travel outside of Canada during consideration of the aforementioned subject.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the events of the last hour and a half have provided an excellent backdrop to the discussion that we hope will continue for the rest of the afternoon and culminate in the acceptance of this motion and an early beginning by the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization of its deliberations.
There are many problems and issues that can be raised in commencing discussion of this motion, particularly the list of items which Your Honour has put together from time to time as subject matter for study by the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. I should like to confine my remarks to brief comments about the process of parliamentary reform in Canada; second, to general comments about the operation of the House of Commons; third, the question period; fourth, Standing Order 43; fifth, the supply procedures; sixth, the committee system; and finally, any other matters that may be of interest to the House.
The process of parliamentary reform in Canada has in recent years become a continuing one. What was once a very sporadic effort has become a continuing process. Hon. members will know that the original rules adopted in 1867 were first revised in 1876. It was then 30 years before further revisions were made in the rules of the House of Commons. The 1906 reforms were followed by further amendments in 1910 and 1913. There were further revisions at approximately 15-year intervals-in 1927, 1940 and 1955.
The present process of continuing reform that is proposed in this motion began about ten years ago. Provisional reforms were adopted in 1964, and work by special committees culminated in the adoption of very major revisions to the rules in 1968. At that time the notion of a permanent Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization was embedded in the Standing Orders. Since 1968, only two amendments have been made to the Standing Orders, the 75a, 75b and 75c rules which are well know to hon. members, and the statutory instruments committee rule.
We, like the British House of Commons, have been constantly aware of the need to reassess and re-examine whatever changes we have made in the recent past, and also to reassess and re-examine old rules that may not have been revised in recent years. It stands as an axiom that the operation of parliament and the operation of the House of Commons requires the constructive co-operation of the members of all parties in the House of Commons. Each one of us may on one day or another behave improperly but we are sustained by the common, constructive balance that is usually maintained by the other members of the House of Commons. Because of that the House is able to operate effectively and to conduct its business.

March 7, 1973
Standing Orders and Procedure
There is great controversy at times in the House. Yesterday was a raw day so far as debate was concerned, but it was a good day for the House of Commons. The strong tempers that were displayed were healthy, but a daily diet of that explosive and tense atmosphere could hardly make for a continuing operation in the House of Commons.
The House is maintained by the Standing Orders, the rules and the Speaker. But as was pointed out in the report of the special committee that travelled to Westminster in 1968, it is also maintained by a subtle understanding of the spirit of parliament that is deeper than the rules and institutions. It is the deepening of that subtle understanding of the spirit of parliament that probably will engage the attention of the members of the standing committee.
The House of Commons is always working against time. The standing committees are always working against time. Time is the most precious commodity; it is precious not only to human beings generally but it seems to be more important to Members of Parliament and to the institution itself. When the members of the special committee visited Westminster in 1968, two observations were heard most frequently from members of the British House of Commons. One was, "We have decided that there are only 365 days in the year". The second was, "We have decided that in debate there comes a time when enough is enough". That was the sentiment that was expressed, not by members of the government but by members of the opposition.
Because of the more frequent changeover in government in the United Kingdom, the people we discussed problems with had experience both in government and in opposition. Their most frequent refrain was, "Time is precious; time is of the essence. There are only 365 days in the year, and if Members of Parliament are going to discharge their responsibilities to their constituents, there must be a predictable, regular way of dealing with parliamentary business".
It was in the light of examining that experience in the United Kingdom as well as our own experience that the special committee made its report to the House, as found in Journals for March 13, 1968. I had the honour of chairing that committee and other hon. members, including the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), were distinguished members. That report, in essence, was the foundation for the general revision of the rules that was undertaken in 1968. It was the foundation and contained the philosophy upon which the subsequent committee built its conclusions.
Referring to the comments heard in Westminster, that there are only 365 days in a year and that time is of the essence, the question has been asked as we look at the calendar on March 7, particularly by the media, "What has been accomplished in this twenty-ninth parliament of Canada?" We have now spent two months in the House of Commons and we have operated under the rules. It is interesting to observe how strongly bound is the operation of this House by the rules which we ourselves adopted.

We spent eight days on the throne speech debate. In view of the fact that almost 100 new members have seats in this House, it would be unrealistic to expect that less than eight days should be spent allowing them and other members to express their views in the House of Commons. As I say, that debate took eight days. Then we spent four days on establishing the prices committee. Was that too long? Surely it was a good debate and brought to the attention of the country a most important question. We spent four days on the controversial unemployment insurance bill removing the so-called ceiling. This provided to members of the House a wide-ranging debate on the whole question of unemployment insurance.
Then the government had to come to the House of Commons looking for $1,300 million in supply. That took nine days. Perhaps that was too long, but certainly it was an opportunity for members to examine the additional spending program of the government in the standing committee. Then, without any time allocation and with the freedom given to hon. members both on second reading and in committee on the clauses and schedules, we used up nine days. Then we had six days on the budget debate.

subtopic: COMMITTEE REVIEW OF AND REPORT ON STANDING ORDERS AND PROCEDURE-AUTHORIZATION TO TRAVEL OUTSIDE OF CANADA DURING STUDY
speechtext: Seven days.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: COMMITTEE REVIEW OF AND REPORT ON STANDING ORDERS AND PROCEDURE-AUTHORIZATION TO TRAVEL OUTSIDE OF CANADA DURING STUDY
speechtext:
It was six days if you do not count yesterday. We had two opposition days, two days on old age security, and four days on the important question of capital punishment. So that is what has taken up the time of the House.
If hon. members want the House to move faster, then they have to strike out days from the budget debate and the address in reply. If they want the House to move even faster, then they have to adopt even more stringent supply provisions than we have at the present time. But that is what the House has done. Those in the media who ask what we have been doing obviously have less than a full understanding of the nature of the House of Commons and the purpose of Members of Parliament. In the words of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker), "It is not a sausage factory." It is not a sausage factory in any sense. That is how we have spent our time since we returned here on January 4.
The immediate cause of accelerating this reference is the operation of the oral question period. Hon. members and Mr. Speaker have on this very day expressed their frustration with the operation of the oral question period. We are not exactly flying blind when we discuss the oral question period in the House of Commons, because on previous occasions the House, through its standing or special committee and in debate in the House, has focused on the operation of the question period. Certainly the 40-minute question period is a result of a recommendation of the standing committee which was unanimously adopted by the House of Commons.
I am sure if hon. members re-examine in the committee the matter of the time of the question period, they will find inexorably that there is no final solution to the operation of the question period by extending it by 10 minutes or 20 minutes. In fact, Mr. Speaker has been more than generous in not seeing the clock during the question period. As I listened to the question period today, I had in front of me the report of a special committee of the House
March 7, 1973

on procedure and organization in April, 1964. That committee was chaired by the then Speaker. That report, which was later concurred in by the House as a whole, had a number of important points to make about the operation of the question period. It reads in part:
Your committee believes that the so-called orders of the day question period should be tightened up.
It continues:
Your committee believes that the implementation of Standing Orders 39(5) and 39-A, as noted above, will provide a basis for more effective use of the right of members to ask questions-
That was a reference to what is now embodied in our practice as the "late show." It goes on to say:
Your committee recommends that the House accept and support the following guidelines. (1) Questions asked prior to orders of the day should be governed by the provisions of Standing Order 39(1).
That is our present Standing Order 39(5) which makes this very clear when it provides:
-questions on matters of urgency may be addressed orally to ministers of the Crown, provided however that, if in the opinion of Mr. Speaker a question is not urgent, he may direct that it be placed on the order paper-
That is the Standing Order and it relates to the question of urgency. The guidelines went on to state:
(2) Such questions should
(a)	be asked only in respect of matters of sufficient urgency and importance as to require an immediate answer;
(b)	not inquire whether statements made in a newspaper are correct;
(c)	not require an answer involving a legal opinion;
(d)	not be asked in respect of a matter that is sub judice;
(e)	not be of a nature requiring a lengthy and detailed answer;
(f)	not raise a matter of policy too large to be dealt with as an answer to a question.
Then recommendation No. 3 reads:
Answers to questions should be as brief as possible, should deal with the matter raised, and should not provoke debate.
We know perfectly well as we observe the question period that these guidelines, especially the one in respect of provoking debate, are observed more in the breach: answers contain debating material and questions contain debating material. It is as certain as the fact that night follows day that any member who adduces an argument or controversy in his question will receive an argument and a debate in the reply if the person replying is at all sensitive to the kind of political forum in which we operate. So it works both ways.
I have every sympathy with the idea of undertaking a further study of the question period, but why do we not go back and look at what we have done already, what we have concurred in already and what we have asked Mr. Speaker to place before us as the rules of the House? I have great sympathy for Mr. Speaker during the daily question period, who with patience attempts to be reconciliatory and solve the impossible task of recognizing every hon. member who rises in his place to ask a question.
Perhaps I may conclude this reference by referring to observations that were made in the report of the special committee of 1968, at page 765. These have not yet been
Standing Orders and Procedure
adopted by the House of Commons. In its report the committee stated as follows:
Another topic that engaged our attention was the question period. At Westminster no questions are asked without notice.
Then it goes on to say:
The effect of a notice requirement in discouraging trivial questions and trivial answers is valued highly by your committee.
We did not recommend the full adoption of the British question period system because I believe our question period is more lively, more entertaining and has many more of the characteristics of the theatre than the British question period. I do believe, however, that we probably could improve the operation of the question period if we relied more on notice, because once a minister has been given notice of a question he is bound, certainly by a sense of duty, to give a much more detailed and much more helpful answer to a question.
I commend the work already done by the committee in respect of the question period, the views of the other committees which examined the matter, and also the possibility that we might take a slight step forward if we adopted the practice of notice, on a trial basis or on a voluntary basis if it is not embedded in the rules.
The suggestion has been made that questions are asked during the oral question period because they are not answered quickly enough by the government when they are placed on the order paper. There may be some validity to that claim, although questions in the oral question period are not entirely for the purpose of seeking information; they are for the constructive purpose of embarrassing the ministry or showing weaknesses, if any exist, in the ministry and scoring political points. However, in my humble opinion the number of questions which appear on the order paper has really gone quite out of sight. If hon. members wish prompt answers to questions which appear on the order paper, it would seem to me that they should be selected in such a manner that pressure could be put on the department to get the answers out as quickly as possible.
In 1968-69 there were 189 sittings which produced 2,723 questions. So far this session we have had 1,420 questions asked in 44 sittings, 329 of which have been answered. This is a very large increase, and the response in 329 cases is not a bad response. Certainly I and other ministers are pushing the departments to get answers out. Sometimes it is like pulling teeth to get information out of departments on time. It is not entirely a matter of ill-will. It seems to me that much has to be done to improve the servicing of parliament by departments. During the last few weeks I have devoted a good deal of time to examining this whole question. It is not an easy one. I believe there is something which can be done to accelerate the process.
Standing Order 43 is a relatively new phenomenon. Why was it brought in? It is a strange thing, but there is a sort of balance which occurs in the House of Commons. When we had Standing Order 26 in respect of questions of urgency, mini-debates developed under the guise of points of order. This was obviously irritating to the Chair and to members of the government, because into the so-called point of order there was bootlegged a whole baggage of political material. This was most unsatisfactory, but that was the way it worked and everybody realized it.

March 7, 1973
Standing Orders and Procedure
The change was not imposed upon hon. members unwillingly. They accepted it. We introduced the "late show" and introduced Standing Order 26 in a new form in order to make it more efficient. Since it does not provide the opportunity for political debate, it is hardly used at all. The technique now has shifted to the use of Standing Order 43. The use of Standing Order 43 has increased very remarkably. In this session, 107 such motions have been presented. Five of these have been accepted for one reason or another. There were 107 matters of "national emergency", or 2.2 "national emergencies" presented every sitting day of the House of Commons. This is the point we have reached. Of these motions, 41 sought to send matters for study, investigation or examination to standing committees of the House, committees that are already sagging from overwork.

speechtext:
The burden will be there. The estimates are ready for the consideration of the committees. I shall say a little more about the committee system later. What do we do about Standing Order 43 every day. I say "No". I become embarrassed saying "No". Why do I say "No".? It is not because I am unsympathetic to the efforts of hon. members to have investigations, but it seems to me that if the House of Commons is to pass a motion it should do so after some deliberation and thought. I instinctively recoil against that as a matter of policy and of inappropriateness for the House of Commons. That is one reason which is perhaps a matter of taste. The other reason is that our operation could become bogged down, because if these motions are to be debated they would supersede government business. They could go on all day, and the next day and the next day-and when would we be able to complete our legislative program and give expression to the needs of the nation as contained in the government's program?
If hon. members continue to put up motions, if that provides an outlet, fine. But we on this side, because of the reasons stated and unless the matter is of universal interest, will continue to use that unhappy expression, "No". It is really not the way to run anything, let alone parliament. I may say that I hope the standing committee will find a way of providing some kind of mini-debate that could capture the interest of the House-occasionally-on the orders of the day or thereabouts, that would give expression to opinions and in which there could be a good interchange. The present system is most unsatisfactory for members as a whole, in my opinion, and if something could be done and the committee could come up with another system, I think it would be most useful.

However, I will not get into an argument on it except to say that under the present supply procedures, patterned basically upon the British system, we send the estimates to the standing committees, rightly or wrongly, and there they are examined, witnesses and ministers are called and individuals present briefs. Many hours are spent on the examination of the estimates. Then they are reported to the House.
It is true that when the guillotine falls it seems appalling that billions of dollars must go through when the Chairman of the committee of the whole House calls the clauses and schedules without debate, but behind that scene- which the right hon. gentleman described as awful-is the enormous amount of study and investigation that took place before. Is it good, or is it bad? I think that is the subject that must be studied.
The hon. member for Peace River mentioned the other day the possibility of bringing some estimates into a committee of the whole. I think that could be examined by the standing committee, because I believe it was beneficial to have had the supply bill for $1.3 billion before the House and before the committee of the whole. I think it provided an excellent debate. It provided hand-to-hand fighting between the opposition and the government, and that is very healthy.
I have not discussed this with anybody else, and I speak only for myself, but I believe that is an aspect that should be considered, namely, whether we should not, with the proper safeguards and maintaining the predictability and the certainty that supply will be granted at certain intervals and the vote will be taken, be given some opportunity under carefully worked out safeguards to debate the estimates in a committee of the whole.
That was one of the issues raised by the hon. member for Edmonton West and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) in December, 1968. The most dedicated advocate of the new supply procedures in that debate was the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who concluded, based upon his experience and the studies in the United Kingdom, as did the government, that this was an
March 7, 1973

improvement. It was a real improvement, in my opinion. But it could be further refined to meet the requirement of examination of estimates in a committee of the whole.
I would like to say a few words about the operation of the committee system. It could be said, with regard to the operation of the committee system, that more changes have been made in the format and the role of House of Commons committees in the past decade than in all the preceding years combined. Beginning in 1962 and culminating in the extensive reorganization of 1968, the committees have taken over more and more of the responsibilities which previously belonged to the House of Commons as a whole.
The rationale of our committee system is fairly straightforward. The committee system allows us to break down the membership of a large group for the sake of efficiency. It allows us to sort our parliamentary workload into more manageable parcels of detail, and it allows members to develop a greater degree of specialization in particular areas of interest. That is the theory, at least.
Hon. members who have been here for the past several years will be aware of the evolution, or perhaps revolution, of our committee system since the early 1960s, but perhaps for new members-there are quite a number of them in the House-I might be able to say a word or two about the major changes that have taken place. The main one, of course, is the requirement that all estimates and all bills, except for budgetary items, be referred to an appropriate committee for detailed study unless the House orders otherwise.
For example, in the last parliament we ordered that a number of bills-I believe the public order bill, and certainly the government reorganization bill-be examined in committee of the whole. Prior to that it was up to the government of the day to decide whether, and when, estimates should go to standing committees. At the same time, the number of standing committees was increased from 14 to 21, and the twenty-second was added in the last session. The average membership was cut in half, from 40 members per committee to about 20.
Another major change was the procedure in changing the membership of committees. Prior to 1968 that was a relatively rigid procedure. Today it happens quickly. You notify the whip and the clerk of the committee, and suddenly you could have a brand new committee.

The point is a valid one. The problem is a different one in a minority government. Some of the points I will put on the record. Some of the information I have here was collected long before this debate, because this was a matter of concern to me before the end of the twenty-eighth parliament. I believe that some of the things I will mention will indicate how dramatically we have changed the committee procedures. It may be that experience will have shown that we have gone a bit too far, and that perhaps we have not gone far enough in other directions. Certainly the increase in the number of committees, as well as the growth in business transacted by committees, places a very heavy burden on Members of Parliament.
It might be of interest to note that in the second session of the twenty-eighth parliament, committees held 759 regular meetings at which legislation, estimates and other matters referred to them by parliament were examined. Contrast this with the second session of the preceding parliament, the twenty-seventh parliament, when the figure was 218. The increase in the number of meetings is in the neighbourhood of 300 per cent.
If we calculate these statistics in hours and relate them to the number of days on which the House sat, the result is even more dramatic. In the two sessions of the twenty-seventh parliament the House sat for 405 days and committees sat for a total of 1,450 hours, approximately-an average of 31 hours of committee meetings for every day that the House sat. In the first two sessions of the twenty-eighth parliament the House sat for 353 days and committees sat for approximately 3,000 hours. This works out to

March 7, 1973
Standing Orders and Procedure an average of 84 hours of committee meetings for every day that the House sat. As a matter of interest, I might note that in the last two sessions of the previous parliament the House sat for 335 days and our committees logged 2,175 hours, for an average of 61 hours for every day the House sat.
So far this session committees are sitting an average of two hours for every day the House sits, which is a pretty high ratio for the beginning of a session when only a few committees are operating. A similar pattern is shown for committee attendances. In the second session of the twenty-seventh parliament there were 3,105 committee attendances by hon. members, and by the second session of the twenty-eighth parliament this had increased to 9,909.
I said earlier that the new committee system places a particularly heavy onus on members. It places an even heavier onus on government members, more so than on non-government members and for understandable reasons. If committee attendance is down and business cannot get under way, that deficiency reflects more upon the government than it does upon the opposition. Regardless of which government has been in office, this has been the case. This government has been in office during the new committee regime and the heavier onus is upon government members, particularly government backbenchers who, with opposition members, are the real workhorses of the committee system.
I will not complain about the present situation. We are facing it as well as we can in manning committees with government members. When ministers, because of other meetings, are not able to sit on standing committees, government members have to carry an extra burden. I will not go into the statistics, but if one examines the attendance record of the last parliament you will see there is no question about it; government members had a very high attendance record, higher than any other group. That is because of the nature of the opposition, the nature of the House, the nature of the political process and for other reasons that I have mentioned.
Committee activity has increased. The volume of work has increased. We have to ask ourselves whether this increased activity on the part of the committee system has detracted from the image and impact of parliament itself. If the answer is yes, then do we want it that way? If it is no, then what do we do to remove some of the difficulties in the present committee system? I have the impression that not all of the changes have lightened the parliamentary load. In some cases they have duplicated the parliamentary load. I have one table here at least, Mr. Speaker, giving a summary comparison of committee activities in the second session of the twenty-seventh parliament and the second session of the twenty-eighth parliament. The figures I have already given show that the workload of committees has increased tremendously, as has the burden on private members.
There is no doubt, in my opinion, that that is one of the reasons why private members in the last parliament and in the present one have asked for greater assistance in their constituencies and in this House. It is because of the demands made upon their time in committees and in the House of Commons.
The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) has asked why I, as government House leader, allow committees to meet while the House is meeting, especially in committee of the whole. There is no way in which we can operate this system unless we permit committees to meet when the House is sitting. In the last session, seven or eight committees met while the House was sitting. I made it a rule that unless there was a desperate emergency, no more than four committees should sit while the House was sitting. This matter must be considered if we are to clear the estimates away and clear away our legislative program. Members not in the House are in committee, or in their offices working, or in their constituencies. That applies to most of them. There are faithful servants of parliament in this House, members who go to committees, who attend in the House and who really make this place live. I will come back to my point. We cannot avoid committees sitting when the House sits.
In the previous parliament we established, with the co-operation of other parties, a scheduling system that attempted to reduce, I think successfully, the number of conflicts that might arise, so that members could be given the opportunity of attending three or four committees without obvious conflict. We are proposing to re-establish that system during the present session. I have many ideas about how the committee system might be changed and improved and I hope at some point to be given the opportunity to make my view known to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization.
I have mentioned some of the problems that have arisen in the operation of our parliamentary system. There are many others. I believe that the work of the procedure and organization committee is of great importance. The work done by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the hon. member for Edmonton West and by others in renovating the rules was prodigious. They sat on subcommittees and brought together all the material and information that resulted in the system we have today. The system is not perfect but it is an improvement.
I hope the committee will take on the big job of doing justice to the items that Mr. Speaker has drawn to our attention. If it has more time, and an appetite for difficulties, it might take on the question of supply procedures and of the committee system. These, however, are very big problems indeed. I apologize to the House for the time I have taken and thank hon. members for paying such close attention to what I have said.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) for his useful and interesting contribution. Speaking as a House leader, I may say that our relations have always been cordial and reasonable, unlike those I experienced before his elevation to this office. While I may say some unpleasant things about the government, I want to except the minister from those statements because in the very difficult hot-house sort of atmosphere in which the various House leaders live he has been very accommodating and reasonable. I extend the same remarks to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), limiting them, of course, to his capacity as House leader. I also extend them to the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) in the same context.
I will not deal with all the questions raised by the minister. Some of my colleagues will deal with certain aspects of the problem to which he referred, and other issues will be mentioned. Before continuing, I wish to refer briefly to the question period. The real problem with the question period stems from the obvious difficulties which the government has constructed for itself. I agree
Standing Orders and Procedure
with the President of the Privy Council that during the question period we are not necessarily seeking factual information. During that period the adversary system under which this House operates comes to the fore. Those who suggest that the adversary system is passe should take a hard look at the structure of our society. For that reason, and for other reasons which the minister mentioned, the question period is the crowning jewel in the diadem of our parliamentary life. I admit that problems have been created during the question period and that members of opposition parties do not always ask questions which are consistent with the rules. However, the real difficulty-I say this genuinely-comes from the application by the government of the three "D's" in government answers: there is too much deception, deviousness and delay.
Your Honour may recall that back in 1958-59 the ministers of the day came to this House well prepared to answer questions. The hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees), who was responsible for several important portfolios in the cabinet of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), always came to this House well briefed. There was hardly a question to which he did not have the answer. The answer did not necessarily satisfy the questioner, but at least he was aware of the subject and had part of the answer. The same cannot be said for members of this government. I suggest, as other hon. members have suggested, that ministers of the Crown in the present government enter the House unprepared to answer a question which must have been obvious, and incapable of giving an answer. The answer may not contain all the facts which may be asked for, but at least it should be adequate.
Time after time we hear the statement, "We will wait until we are able to find the information and the hon. member will be informed in due course." These are the characteristics of those on the treasury benches which drive members of the opposition to frustration, anger and cause them to perpetrate, sometimes unconsciously and certainly unwillingly, infractions of the rules with regard to the question period. That is all I am going to say about it. I think the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) will deal with this later. It is a very important part of our parliamentary life. It is the time when the government, under the full glare of the spotlight of publicity, must meet the challenge, scrutiny and questioning of hon. members from all sides of the House who have been sent here to deal with government problems, government delays and government prejudices.
I am sometimes taken aback by the calm assumption of so many people, including many Members of Parliament, as to the sacrosanct quality and irreversible nature of the democratic process and rule of law as if having once achieved these things, sometimes by force, they will never be lost or even diminished, that the present eclipse of parliament and its function is merely temporary. These are dangerous assumptions to make. Those who believe in them are living in a fool's paradise. The human race has taken over half a million years to achieve the present position, and democratic institutions are 100 or 200 years old. This is certainly not a very long time in the context of

March 7, 1973
Standing Orders and Procedure the history of mankind, certainly not long enough to have become part of the bloodstream and nerve centre of social evolution.
This very delicate and fragile institution is under continuous attack from executive government. The ever-hungry, monolithic monster of bureaucracy keeps chewing away at the few rights which remain to parliament, and on these they are receiving the very loyal and enthusiastic support of the elected branch of the executive, the cabinet. Certainly this is the case in Canada.
I could not do better than chronicle some of the highlights of this session's activities as a litany of the incidents of use or abuse of the executive power, uses that have caught the attention of this House over the past two months. There is the Vietnamese situation wherein the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) calmly asserted that parliament may be given some very brief and innocuous right of discussion long after the event. He refused to bring back for discussion and decision the motion launched under his name.
There is also the matter of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. There is the question of not only the deprivation of the right of scrutiny of this House by taking away certain changes in this legislation, but what we see going on day after day and what has been the subject of a very searching and intelligent cross-examination today as to the kind of rules and changes which are being made at the whim of the minister.
There are serious problems regarding unemployment insurance. I know that the government faces some of those. Why in heaven's name does the government not seize the nettle, bring the question into this House and let the House decide? We are the people who have been elected by our constituents all over Canada. We know what will be the impact of programs of this kind and of changes that are envisaged. Let this House look at the situation and decide.
The department of immigration has given away hundreds of millions of dollars to LIP and OFY programs which are sanctioned and spent without one bit of approval by this House until long after the event. With regard to the auto pact, all we are able to do is contained in the question period with the not-so-artful dodging of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie). Hundreds of millions of dollars are being spent, and if we include the provincial contribution it is probably billions of dollars, on the construction of airports for which this parliament is not asked for one bit of advice. There is the James Bay project, which engaged the attention of the House today, and other matters.
These indicate beyond any doubt what is happening. They demonstrate the means employed by this government to downgrade, bypass, ignore or overrun the legislature. In each instance it is an example of the mishandling of arbitrary executive authority to create or intensify problems. This is not only happening in Canada. In the United States today, the President is locked in a conflict with Congress as to appropriations. There were the problems with regard to the Viet Nam war, the resolution following the Bay of Tonkin incident and the powers given to the President at that time. We are not isolated in these instances, although we have a government com-

posed of people who have become very skilful in their adoption of these executive powers.
It would be bad enough to surrender more and more power to the government even where the exercise of these powers results in greater efficiency and brings benefits to the people who are ruled, but such is not the case, certainly not in Canada where we see misrule, inefficiency and incompetence grow in direct proportion to the increase in authoritarianism. This debate is an opportunity for members of the House to dig in their heels and say, "Enough!"
This minority government seemed to give us one last chance to regain some of the rights which had been wrenched away, but in light of the conduct of my friends in the New Democratic Party, I am beginning to wonder. I say as rationally as I can and quite objectively, it is becoming quite clear that we do not have a minority government in this House. We have an actual, practising coalition, so much so that I sincerely wonder about the right that may well be asserted by the New Democratic Party to move a motion on an allotted opposition day. I point out to members of this House that under the Standing Orders, this right is reserved to those who are, and I quote, "in opposition to the government". There is a strong reason to suspect, and certainly Your Honour can take judicial notice of this, that the members of the New Democratic Party are anything but in opposition to the government.
I have heard it said by both the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and by the leader of the New Democratic Party that they are going to try to make parliament work. I welcome this statement. I try to believe it. I work hard at believing it. However, having observed these distinguished gentlemen in action, I have my doubts. Making parliament work for them seems to have a very different meaning than it has for me and most members of this House. For the Prime Minister it means making it work in such a way that he can look in the mirror every day and ask, "Mirror, mirror on the wall, am I still the biggest of them all?" then come here and take his place in the Prime Minister's seat. For the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) it is not quite as satisfactory. For him, making parliament work means his ability to come into the House every day, look at the Prime Minister sitting in his seat and say to himself, "There, by the grace of David Lewis, sits Pierre Elliott Trudeau." The more I watch these two distinguished members of this House-I say this with due apology to both of them-the more I notice how much they resemble each other.
The fact of the matter is, there has developed a sort of collusive understanding to deny to the Progressive Conservative party, Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, all real opportunity to have any point of view accepted by the House. The events of the last few weeks have demonstrated this to be the case beyond any shadow of doubt. So much so, indeed, that if our party were to put forward a motion proposing a revision of the prayer with which the proceedings of this House open, I anticipate that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and the leader of the New Democratic Party would rise in their places and scream that this, too, indicated a lust for power in our ranks.
March 7, 1973

Despite these misgivings, I have the duty to put before the House for the consideration of the committee on procedure some views with respect to what might be examined by the committee, on what should be done and on what course might be taken with regard to this motion. Certainly I agree with the President of the Privy Council that the whole question of supply and of opposition days as related to the consideration of departmental estimates ought to be closely examined in light of the experience of the last four or five years. This experience demonstrates beyond any reasonable doubt that committees can never be a substitute or an alternative for the House of Commons. They must be ancilliary to rather than in substitution for this chamber.
I do not say that committees cannot be used as an excellent means of providing an occasion for the examination of witnesses, of hearing evidence from ministers and from senior officials, of allowing the presentation of briefs by interested citizens throughout the country, because they are valuable means of obtaining the views of representatives of sectors of the public affected by issues which demand parliamentary attention. These things simply cannot be done in the House itself. Committees, used in the way I have described, are extremely effective in conjunction with the operation of the Commons.
I have already suggested, however, that the right should be reserved to this House, either in committee of the whole or through the revival, in a limited way, of the committee of supply, to deal with several departments of government, those departments to be selected by the opposition. The leader of the House has been good enough to indicate some acceptance of this view, subject, I agree, to certain safeguards as to the time to be taken and the manner of the proceedings. I should like to make a firm suggestion to the President of the Privy Council right now. We would not be unwilling to agree, as an experiment, during this session, even while the standing committee on procedure is considering the matter, to allocate some of the opposition days during which the estimates of several departments might be examined. Hon. members to my left, as well as members of the Creditiste party, might agree to co-operate, and maybe one or two government days could be made available for this purpose.
The committee on procedure would then have an opportunity to examine the experiment actually in progress and be in a better position to bring proposals back to the House. The government has nothing to lose by accepting a proposition of this kind. It might be a useful way of coming to grips with this question. I agree with the minister that there has been a good deal of misunderstanding shown in the media and elsewhere as to the manner in which the present rules apply. Among the most important functions of this House is the granting of supplies of money to government to enable it to carry out its programs and operations. It is at this point that the right of the opposition to voice grievances and seek redress is available to hon. members. But these opposition days upon which such grievances can be raised are not chosen by us. They are granted by the government. The government has every right to say to us: You will take this day, or that day. It is true that the minister has done his best to be accommodating, but the government has the right to
Standing Orders and Procedure
say to the opposition: These are the days on which you will bring forward your motions.
The problem too often arises that on those particular days reports are not yet forthcoming from committees examining the estimates. For example, the estimates are just going before the committees, now. It might well be that intelligent and hard working opposition members will ascertain, having followed the evidence and crossexamination of witnesses in those committees, that there are certain aspects of the estimates which might well be the subject of an opposition day. But this is not an opportunity which is presented to us at the present time. One of the steps which might be taken is this: the days might be fixed by the government in consultation with the opposition so that at least we should be able, from time to time, to indicate much more strongly than at present that we have certain views of our own as to what days should be selected.
We moved a motion last Monday and we moved a motion yesterday, not necessarily because we wanted those particular days but because those days had been chosen by the government. The choice of subject matter was ours, of course. When the Minister of Finance was dealing with the motion yesterday he was, in my opinion, guilty of the most nauseating and juvenile hypocrisy when he suggested we were taking up the time of the House improperly by dealing with the motion and, in effect, preventing the House from attending to other matters.
Mr. Speaker, we were debating that motion yesterday because the government had directed that yesterday was a day upon which we would be able to bring down a motion on an opposition day. The reason is plain. Two or three days ago the government introduced supplementary estimates. Those estimates must be passed by the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates and reported to the House. Only after this has been done can there be an appropriation bill voting supply to the government. Considering the course on which we are now launched, this cannot be done until the last of the seven opposition days has gone by. So the government must ensure that those seven days are taken before the end of March, perhaps even earlier than March 26, if my recollection is correct, bearing in mind that the appropriation bill must go to the Senate, and one never knows how long the other place will take to consider a bill dealing with estimates.
I will go further. Let us admit it, on many of the opposition days when motions have been put down which do not involve the question of confidence, no matter how entertaining the subject matter, no matter how effective the debate, no matter what status is enjoyed by the hon. members who participate, by the time three speeches have been made all interest peters out. There have been one or two exceptions, but that is our experience. Interest falls off, not only among those whose duty it is, or should be, to report these proceedings, but among many hon. members as well.
I should like to suggest to the committee on procedure that consideration is given to making it possible for there to be a vote at the end of each of the opposition days. I do not suggest that each one of these will be a non-confidence motion. I am in definite agreement that there must be some limitation in that regard. But I do suggest that if

March 7, 1973
Standing Orders and Procedure there were to be a vote with respect to each of these opposition days, it would permit all members-that is, all members genuinely in opposition to the government-to bring down motions and compel the House to divide on the issue.
As I have pointed out, this need not involve the question of confidence. It may well be that some of them will be passed. However, I think it would present an opportunity that does not exist now and would raise these opposition days' discussions to a level they do not possess at the present time. I realize there are some practical difficulties, but it would do a lot to improve interest. I hope the committee will look at that issue.
Another issue is one we have discussed in the House but which has never erupted openly. I refer to what we in this party assert is the sole prerogative of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, namely, to introduce motions of non-confidence. This results from the procedure which was adopted on supply days. If there is to be a motion of non-confidence, I submit with respect it is the prerogative of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition to so move. This leaves the other opposition parties quite free to move amendments. This was the procedure adopted when we had supply motions and it worked very effectively and was satisfactory to all parties. I hope that the committee on procedure will take a look at this matter as well.
The matter of supply relates directly to problems that have been experienced in the operation of the committees. The minister recognized this during the course of his speech and some of my colleagues will have more to say on the matter. There is no doubt at all that our experiences over the last few years have not been happy ones. For example, there are questions such as the size of committees, the number of members and committees, the chairmanship of committees, areas of responsibility, the right to make reports, the right of debating and dealing with reports, and the opportunity to come to a firm decision in the House on such reports rather than have them expire on the order paper as is now the case.
Once a motion to adopt a report has been debated for one day, it becomes a government order and it is only at the option of the government that it can be revived. This is a highly unsatisfactory system, one that is most frustrating to members who have a keen interest in the subject matter. I think it should not be possible for the government to frustrate and to deprive the members of the House who have served on the committee in question of the chance to have the House debate the committee report to a conclusion so a decision may be arrived at.
I should like to make a strong suggestion regarding a new facet of the committee system. I would suggest that the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization collaborate with the Joint Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments with a view to building up a jurisprudence for the operation of that committee. In my opinion, this joint committee could well become, depending upon the wisdom of the members who compose the committee from both places, the chairmanship of the committee and the tolerance of and assistance

given by members of this House and the other place, the most important committee in this parliament.
However, some rules will have to be laid down, and probably introduced into the Standing Orders of this House and of the other place, permitting the joint committee once it gets underway to bring into the House for debate from time to time some of its reports, views and recommendations regarding its review of government by order in council and decree. There will have to be some way by which parliament, and certainly this House, can under certain circumstances have a power of review, with even a power of amendment if necessary and of disallowance where it has been established that there have been abuses by government when it proceeds to govern by way of decree, order in council and regulation.
I should now like to make a few proposals regarding the rights of private members. I do not think there is any doubt that there is a great deal of frustration and unhappiness on the part of private members, particularly the new members, with regard to the limited extent that they are able to debate to the point of decision in the House measures and proposals that they put forward in the form of private members' public bills or notices of motions. I say this recognizing, of course, that there must always rest with the government in the main the right to initiate legislative and spending proposals.
Under the constitution and in accordance with the practice that has been built up in this House, we have the safeguard that no member of the House other than a minister of the Crown can introduce measures which have any monetary consequences. In order to comply with the constitution and the practice of the House, there must be a recommendation by the Crown in this regard. So I suggest there would be no harm done if private members' public bills were allowed to come to a decision. The difficulty is, of course, as the minister said, finding the time. I suggest we can find means to permit, at least in some number, private members' public bills being debated to the point of decision. I think we should get away from the involuntary hypocrisy, the frustration and fraud that exists in the House today-through no one's fault- because of the practices that have been built up.
I think this can be done in such a way as not to deprive the government of the time it requires to transact government business. My view has been, at least over the last two years, that taking the hour between 5 and 6 p.m. for private members' business often results in a loss of time. I can think of innumerable occasions when the House was debating a government measure, every opportunity for debate had about been exhausted, and where I am convinced that had the debate continued until six o'clock it would have been concluded and the question put or the bill passed without question.
I suggest that the committee give some consideration to retaining the hour between five and six o'clock for government business and that private members' hour be taken either from 7.30 to nine o'clock or from 9.30 to 11 p.m., giving an hour and a half instead of the hour as at present. I must say at this point that I think there has to be some kind of limitation on the number of private members' public bills that are in fact introduced. I am not going to deal with this arbitrarily or lay down any specific

number, but I do think that this business of one member putting down 30, 40 or 50 bills in the hope that he may-

speechtext:
I recognize that, but I should also like to see in the rules some limit placed on the number of bills. Then I propose that there be a ballot for, say, 20 bills. Or better still, we could follow the British and, I think, the Australian practice and have a ballot for 20 members. Those who were successful in the draw would receive a certain priority on the clear understanding, through a change in the Standing Orders, that the bills that they see fit to introduce would, within the one and a half hour period devoted to private members' public business, be brought to a clear decision. All questions would have to be put within that hour and a half so that second reading would be completed.
I now go beyond that, Mr. Speaker. I would assume that these bills would go to a committee where some would fall by the wayside. I would not expect that those 20 bills would pass the acid test of committee approval. A fair guess would be that ten might emerge from the committee. Then ten days should be provided for another draw when the private members' public bills which were completed in the committee would be brought into the House for report stage and third reading.
This would mean that over the course of the average parliament of four sessions, we might well see anywhere from 20 to 35 private members' public bills pass this House at all stages. I do not know what would happen to them in the other place. I have every reason to believe this would be of great inspiration and would do a great deal, not only for private members but for the people in the country who delegate their members to bring forward certain issues in an attempt to obtain remedial legislation. No one would suffer and the government would lose no time, as I have worked this out. Some hon. members would be compelled to sit additional hours from time to time. I do not suggest this should be every day, but I put it forward in the hope that the committee will look at my suggestion.
I am going to direct my attention now to one more question before I sit down. In doing so, I am not in any sense underrating the other issues which have been referred to in the terms of reference. Other hon. members will deal with them. I would point out that there is available, through the courtesy of the Chair, a direction in the terms of reference, if one goes behind it, to the time and place in Hansard where these issues were discussed. That is a starting point when the committee considers these other issues.
I want to deal with the question of reasoned amendments. I am particularly concerned about this, because of the nature and the type of legislation which is now brought forward by governments. In the earlier days, when the precedents in respect of reasoned amendments were laid down, an examination of the kind of bill then brought forward would show a rather simple measure with a clearly defined principle, in this country and else-
Standing Orders and Procedure
where, and it was easy to say that this was the principle involved, have a debate on second reading and when the legislature passed or rejected the measure it was dealing with a clearcut and discernible principle. That is not the case today. Today, virtually all legislative bills are composite and deal with a number of subject matters which are complex and frequently highly technical in nature. Virtually all include very large regulation-granting sections. It is just impossible to say in respect of most of these bills that there is only one principle involved.
I do not wish to take up the time of the House, because one need only go down the index of statutes to see the kind of legislation that is deemed necessary today to introduce to this House. For that reason I have sought, together with some of my colleagues in all opposition parties, over the last few years to move the type of reasoned amendment which would permit a division in the House on second reading beyond the simple yea or nay limitation which is now being inflicted upon us, the motion for six months' hoist or the other motion which can be moved in referring the subject matter to a committee.
I am sure it will not have escaped the attention of the Chair, as it has not escaped my attention and the attention of my colleagues in all opposition parties, that this has been done and that the Chair has so far both determinedly and successfully been able to resist our efforts to put forward reasoned amendments of the type frequently accepted in the United Kingdom. Yet the anomaly, Mr. Speaker, is that the precedents in Erskine May's which have been preserved and brought forward into Beau-chesne's are precisely the same precedents which today exist in England.
I have put on the record here on a number of occasions a dozen or more illustrations of amendments of the type which have been moved and accepted in the United Kingdom, yet attempts to move similar motions here have been rejected. Frequently the government has resorted to what I call the nit-picking rule. I say with regret that such arguments have been too often accepted by the Chair in rejecting these amendments.
The plain fact is that many bills introduced in this House deal with a number of subjects and in many instances we accept particular parts as being proposals that are necessary, essential and good for the country, our constituencies and the economy; but the bills often contain other measures which are repugnant, do nothing for the country and to which we object. What is the House to do on second reading, in that event? If we are limited to the simple procedures I have detailed to the House, we must accept or reject the entire bill. If we reject it, then we reject some proposals we find quite acceptable. If we accept it, we include in it certain proposals which we do not like and feel should not be included.
The reasoned amendments which are put in the United Kingdom so often-I have placed these on the record of this House-usually say that while accepting the principle, or the need to do certain things, the House rejects other aspects, philosophies or principles of the bill. These amendments are very simply worded and permit the House to have an interesting and informative debate on a particular issue, and they permit the opposition party or a

March 7, 1973
Standing Orders and Procedure member ot the government to compel the House to divide on the issue.
I would therefore ask the standing committee which will look into this matter very seriously to consider the question of reasoned amendments. There is just no way in which the House, asked to deal with the kind of detailed and complex legislative proposals which come before us, can cope with these on second reading. In fact, I should like to go further: I see no reason why we should not consider the proposition that second reading be limited only to reference to a committee. Why should there be a question of principle involved at all? Why not say second reading is merely the examination of a piece of legislation and an opportunity to debate it at first blush, with the only result being the passage of the motion and reference to the committee?
Under the procedures on the basis of which we operate today, it is only after a bill has gone to a standing committee, perhaps been amended, and comes back to the House for the report stage and third reading that this House sees the final form completely before it and completely exposed. At that time, of course, there is no escape and hon. members must divide on the issue if they see fit. I would suggest that the committee might very seriously consider recommending that second reading be relegated to a much less important phase of the legislative process than is the case today.
Before I leave that matter there is a related aspect which I should like to raise. It is probably not squarely within the terms of reference, but because we have had this dispute in a good humoured way between the Chair and hon. members it seems to me there should be some way in which the House might, where there is a continuing division of opinion between the Chair and hon. members, be provided an opportunity, without going through the process of recommendations from the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization, to obtain the views of members of the House. By this I mean that the last substantive rule changes of any consequence were made in 1968, and we are now in the year 1973.
I would like to think that even if an election should intervene, the deliberations of this committee would be forwarded on to the committee which will be established in the next parliament. It may well be a year and a half from now before any rule changes have been recommended by the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization and have become part of the operative conduct of this House. There is a very simple procedure which I would hope might be used. I want to make abundantly clear that I am not suggesting that we revert to the old practice of appeals to rulings of the Speaker. However, I believe there is a very simple way to make use of the device of a stated case. If we do not do this, I think there is a danger from the procedural aspect because the House might become locked in positions of absolute inflexibility, which is not a good thing.
If an issue should arise it might be that the Chair itself might direct a stated case. It may be that a minimum number of members would be required to give a reply, but the process of a stated case would be that the Chair

would state the facts, the statutes and the precedents which prompted the Chair to give a decision, and there would be limited debate. On that basis I think there would be a freshness and vitality in our proceedings which seem to be lacking at the present time. In this way there would be guidance to the Chair in respect of making decisions and giving rulings on this aspect.
This has been a limited contribution, although I am afraid it has been long as to time. This is one of the difficulties in this House. As the President of the Privy Council pointed out, there is so much to do and so little time in which to do it. The government might give consideration to the idea of a new calendar which would provide 15 months and 36 hours in each day.
I come now to a proposition I have previously put forward in this House. I agree with those who say that this is not a House of perfection. I would like to add that I hope it never will be. We are here to serve as a mirror for the hopes, aspirations, fears and anxieties of the people we represent. We are these people, warts and all, with their defects as well as their genius. Despite that, there is far more hope to be found in the House of Commons, with all its imperfections, comprised as it is of men and women who are in continuous and daily contact with the people in their constituencies in all parts of Canada, than in all the ivory palaces of the bureaucracy filled with the theoreticians, the bureaucrats, the schemers and the fixers.
The problem we face, as always, in so arranging our rules of conduct in this House with due regard to the adversary system is that our debates and our decisions will truly reflect the demands of the aggregate of all our constituents in Canada, for within them lies the true, ultimate political wisdom.
