speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with some trepidation this afternoon following such distinguished hon. members as the two House leaders who preceded me. I cannot rival them in experience and I certainly cannot rival them in eloquence. In addition, according to the rules of this House I cannot even rival them in length of time. I do not wish to detract from the contribution they made by mentioning the length of time they spoke, because I believe the information presented to us by the government House leader and the suggestions presented to us by the House leader of the Official Opposition will be of considerable use to the committee when it examines the procedures and organization of the House.
My party welcomes this opportunity to discuss procedure and organization. It is entirely appropriate that at least once in a parliament this House should take the time to examine its method of operation with a view to ensuring that we are capable of so ordering our business and
Standing Orders and Procedure
our time that we are able to discharge our duty to the Canadian electorate with the greatest possible efficiency and effectiveness.
I use the word "efficiency" with some reluctance because all too often critics of parliament tend to base their assessment of its efficiency upon criteria which are better suited to time, speed and motion studies in industry than to a legislative body. Parliament should not be viewed as some kind of legislative assembly line producing bill after bill and the only judgment made upon its efficiency being the time it takes to complete the process. Rather, parliament's efficiency in terms of legislation should be judged upon the degree to which opportunity is given for the various views within the country to be expressed and considered, the degree to which items before the House relate to the needs and desires of the people of the country, needs and desires both real and imagined, and the degree to which the resulting legislation satisfies those needs and desires.
I would hope that in its re-examination of our rules and procedures, the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization will take considerable pains to ensure that its work is based upon a realistic assessment of the current role of individual members and a realistic appraisal of what we can legitimately expect the legislative assembly to accomplish in today's positive state, rather than upon theoretical expressions of the role of the legislature and its members or upon a nostalgic desire to return to the good old days or to some golden age of parliamentary democracy which probably has never existed in any case.
Traditionally, the role of the legislature has been to devise laws for the governing of the country, to decide upon means of raising the revenue necessary to implement those laws, and to supervise expenditure in order to ensure that money is spent in a way desired by the legislature. Traditionally, also, the legislature was to provide a means of redress of grievance for citizens adversely affected by the state.
In a modern state, because of the multiplicity of its interests and the highly technical considerations involved in meeting those interests, initiative in three of the four areas mentioned above-legislation, taxation and supervision of expenditures-has gravitated almost naturally into the hands of the executive, the cabinet and the bureaucracy which serves it. I doubt very much that we could operate effectively as government were the situation otherwise. Thus, a realistic assessment of the potentiality of the legislature would seem to be that it be able to offer advice to the executive in each of these three areas- legislation, taxation and supervision of expenditures- advice which would, hopefully, be listened to by the government, and that in addition the legislature be able to effectively hold the government accountable for governmental action.
It is in this sense of accountability that I believe parliament should exert its control of the executive. Bernard Crick in his book "The Reform of Parliament" had this to say about parliamentary control:
The only meanings of parliamentary control worth considering, and worth the House spending much of its time on are those which do not threaten the parliamentary defeat of a government, but

March 7, 1973
Standing Orders and Procedure
which help to keep it responsive to the underlying currents and the more important drifts of public opinion. All others are purely antiquarian shufflings. It is wholly legitimate for any modern government to do what it needs to guard against parliamentary defeat; but it is not legitimate for it to hinder parliament, particularly the opposition, from reaching the public ears effectively as it can. Governments must govern in the expectation that they can serve out their statutory period of office, that they can plan-if they choose-at least that far ahead, but that everything they do may be exposed to the light of day and that everything they say may be challenged in circumstances designed to make criticism as authoritative, informed and as public as possible.
Thus, I would like to assert that in looking over rules and procedures in the House the standing committee should dedicate its efforts to ensuring that parliamentary control of the sort mentioned by Bernard Crick in that passage is possible. Similar considerations apply to the individual member. His traditional role was to devise policy for the government of the country, to decide upon means of raising revenue and to supervise expenditures. Those were considered to be his major duties and they were expected to occupy the bulk of his time in this institution.
Therefore, the procedures and the organization and the services provided to members were designed to assist them in fulfilling those specific roles. Moreover, the services, organization and procedures were to a large extent determined in a period when the House dealt with matters lacking the complexity of the issues with which the House is obliged to deal today. The role of the member has changed. More and more of the member's time is devoted to assisting individual constituents with their problems, and this fact must be acknowledged when changes in services and rules of procedure and organization are contemplated by the standing committee.
With that sort of general approach as background to my remarks, I would like to offer some fairly precisely defined suggestions for the consideration of the standing committee, suggestions which I believe would greatly assist this chamber and its individual members effectively to discharge their duties as currently defined by practice rather than theory.
First, following the line taken by the two previous speakers, I should like to take some time to look at the question period which is one of the greatest causes of frustration to all members of the House, I might add, especially to backbench members. This situation is extremely unfortunate because the question period is potentially one of the most effective means of exercising control over executive actions in the sense of bringing them to the light of day; it is also one of the most effective potential methods of securing redress of grievances.
It is my impression that over the past number of years the question period has developed into an occasion for a mini-debate which is invariably dominated by the front-bench members of all parties. It is no longer an occasion for eliciting information from the government or drawing to the attention of the government the adverse effects of their policies and the shortcomings in their administration of those policies on a broad range of issues.
Beyond that, the question period should be a much more effective vehicle than it is now for drawing to the attention of the government matters of national policy and the results of national policy which are of concern to

individual members and their constituents. It is in this regard, with a view to increasing the number of potential participants in each question period and to increasing the variety of issues which might be raised in the House in any question period, that I would strongly urge the standing committee to give serious consideration to discovering a means of permitting Mr. Speaker to limit the number of supplementary questions permitted an individual member and the number of supplementary questions permitted on any given topic on any given day.
Another current cause of frustration for backbench members arising out of the current method of organizing our question period is that many questions are taken as notice by ministers. This is an entirely acceptable procedure, but its difficulty is that in order to ultimately obtain an answer to the question put, the member must utilize another occasion on which he must be successful in catching Mr. Speaker's eye to again pose the same question. In circumstances where the member cannot legitimately expect to catch Mr. Speaker's eye more than once or twice a week, if that, and where he may be interested in a good many more subjects than the one involved in his original question, he must forgo the opportunity to demonstrate his interest in additional areas of concern if he is to obtain an answer to the question asked in the first instance.
I would strongly urge that the practice be adopted of placing on the order paper any question taken as notice by a minister. It should be placed on the order paper as a starred question, and such starred questions should be considered as additional to the three starred questions which currently each hon. member, at any given time, is permitted to place on the order paper. Such a practice would ensure that members would obtain an answer without having to ask the same question repeatedly, and at the same time it would avoid the kind of problem which Mr. Speaker encounters when a minister, after answering a question, launches into a reply to another question asked several days previously, using the preface, "While I am on my feet, Mr. Speaker-". I will not go further into the question period at this stage.
In the final analysis, the success of the question period depends on the wisdom and forebearance of the members of the House. It also depends upon their courtesy. One of the greatest handicaps to the question period being effective is the practice that is employed by a considerable number of members in all parties, raising spurious points of order and spurious points of privilege as vehicles for asking more supplementaries, or of raising another matter, all to the disadvantage of other members of the House. We need to be self-regulating in that regard. I would strongly urge the standing committee to study seriously the two specific suggestions which I have made.
Is is only slightly overdrawing the case to say that within the last 125 years we have gone full circle from legislatures being relatively weak advisers to and opposition for government to full legislative control and responsibility, and back again to the situation where a legislature is in fact of only peripheral importance in the governing of the nation.
March 7, 1973

Parliament stands in danger of becoming, as has the monarchy, a largely honorific element in the constitution. I make these remarks in no partisan sense. What has happened in Canada is happening throughout the world. The decline of the power of parliament in relation to the cabinet and to the first minister has been allowed to proceed as far as it has, in part because the process was neither the result of stated policy nor, for the most part, of conscious effort. The change is, rather, the result of innumerable individual decisions made on a pragmatic basis over a long period of time and as a consequence of two major developments-the growth in the scope of responsibility of the modern state and the marked strengthening of party discipline which has taken place since confederation.
Whatever the reasons for the change, whatever the reasons for the phenomenon of the decline in power of the legislative arm of government in relation to the executive arm, it is absolutely necessary for us to use every means at our disposal to attempt to halt the trend, if not reverse it. I make this assertion, not because of some antiquarian concern for the dignity of the House but, rather, because the more power becomes concentrated, the less responsive is the government to the felt needs of the people. I have no doubt that this very concentration of power is producing the current, entirely legitimate demands for "people power" in democratic states and is producing, as well, some of the less savoury aspects of that movement.
It is within this context that I wish to discuss some suggestions for change in our current committee system, which I hope will be considered by the standing committee, because I see the committee system as having the greatest immediate potential for beginning the process of re-establishing, in fact, the control of the executive by the legislature or, to put it another way, of ensuring the responsibility and accountability of the cabinet to parliament. Our present committee system was set up in 1965 on a trial basis and was given formal approval by the House in December, 1968. The committee system, I think I can assert without fear of contradiction, has not worked quite as we had hoped it would. I think I can also assert without fear of contradiction that the time has come to give it a thorough re-examination. In establishing the committee system, parliament gave up a number of its more effective controls over executive powers, such as the study of estimates in committee of the whole, at which time grievances could be raised with the government with some effect. We have lost that control and the committee system has not replaced it with another equally effective method of control.
Parliament's power to supervise has declined because of the increasing demands being made on its time, and because its members are representative men and women best equipped to deal with general principles, broad objectives and fundamental issues. It is not a technical body. When it comes to dealing with technical legislation there exists a substantial information gap between the private member and the cabinet minister. Cabinet ministers can draw upon the talents and resources of the legions of public service experts, which the cabinet controls, for necessary information in any field. With rare exceptions, such as the audit office, parliament can call upon no such able assistance. The result is that debates in
Standing Orders and Procedure
the House tend to be rather unequal and the ability of parliament to assess adequately and scrutinize every government action is severely reduced.
Committees would have the potential to remedy this situation if their memberships were more stable. I believe this is something to which the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) referred. In other words, if Members of Parliament remained on a given committee for a longer period of time, were not shuffled about so frequently, and if there were periodic adjournments of the House for the purpose of enabling committees to do their work, they could help remedy this situation. With respect to periodic adjournments of the House in order to allocate time to committee work, a number of different systems have been suggested. I will not go into them now, Mr. Speaker. They are known to the members of the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. I simply content myself with saying the committee would be well advised to seek the most satisfactory means of providing committees with the time they need to do their work properly without the interference of other duties, such as attendance in this chamber.
It is with the same end in view, that of enhancing the ability of committees to reduce the information gap between parliament and government, that I would recommend that committees be provided with adequate staff support. I refer especially to research staff who would possess the expert knowledge necessary to assist Members of Parliament in preparing themselves for their various committee duties. The value of such staff has been made manifestly obvious in the case of external affairs and national defence by the work of Mr. Peter Dobel and the parliamentary research centre. I would strongly urge the standing committee to examine the relationship of Mr. Dobel to that particular committee with a view to seeing if similar principles could be applied to other committees of the House.
There is a problem in deciding whether such staff should be permanent of rotating, assigned to a single committee or moved from committee to committee as required, whether the research staff should be the creature of the House or whether it should be of a semiautonomous nature as is the case with the parliamentary research centre. I tend to opt for a permanent staff with some degree of autonomy, but the point is that able research staff is urgently required by committees. That is the point I wish to establish at this time, and I hope the standing committee will examine it during its deliberations.
A related suggestion is that a standing committee be permitted, as a matter of course, to act as a committee of inquiry. For example, I see no reason why the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, in the situation now confronting the nation, should not find it to be a normal part of its duties to inquire into the relationship between inflation and unemployment, or into the possible effects of the American DISC program upon our economy and, accordingly, make appropriate policy recommendations in these fields. Such a development would have two major beneficial effects, the first of better equipping parliament to assess government policy decisions in these areas by having committees engage in fun-

March 7, 1973
Standing Orders and Procedure damental research work and, secondly, of providing government with the advice of Members of Parliament who, while they might not possess in all cases, in fact usually never possess, the same technical competence as the government's expert advisers, can present their advice from the point of view of persons representing constituents, persons who must be responsible to the electorate.
There would be no necessity, in keeping with the traditions of the parliamentary system, for a government to implement policy recommendations presented by a committee. But at least the committee should have the power to make suggestions to the government, and the government should present some response to the committee. That does not happen at the moment.
We must also seek ways and means to make it impossible for a government to ignore the recommendations of a committee. To this end, the standing committee should give consideration to the proposition that it should be made mandatory for a motion of concurrence to be moved in connection with all committee reports and that such a motion shall be deemed to be debatable. This would provide two salutory effects: first, the recommendations of the committee would be aired in public; second, if concurrence were granted, the government would be forced to explain its reasons for failing to act upon a recommendation of the committee. It would have to pay more attention to what the committee did.
Obviously, this suggestion poses problems with regard to the time of the House. Some means would have to be discovered for limiting debate. Perhaps a Standing Order could provide that only a certain number of reports could be debated in a session or, more likely, an over-all time limit for such debates could be established and the opposition given the choice of which reports to debate within that time. Perhaps more allotted days could be granted, with the express purpose of such debates in mind. Once again, Mr. Speaker, the actual technique decided upon does not concern me at this stage so much as the principle. I am willing to trust the wisdom of the standing committee and let it go into the details as to how such a device might be established. However, I think it is necessary.
I also wish to suggest that in order to strengthen the impact of committee reports, committees be required to prepare at the end of each session a running record, covering previous sessions as well, of the recommendations it has made to the government and the action the government has taken on those recommendations. Such a record could be a powerful weapon in the hands of individual Members of Parliament determined to make the government take some account of the work done in committees. If, for example, over a period a committee made 27 recommendations and the government did not do anything about them, the government's failure to act could be devastating ammunition in the hands of opposition members.
The idea is not original. It is derived from the practice of the British public accounts committee which each year prepares an epitome of proposals. It is also the practice in Westminster that after a committee makes a recommen-

dation the ministry, not long after, provides that committee with a response to that recommendation. In addition, the committee is informed of any action that the minister might take on the recommendation, if it has merit. If it has no merit, the committee is told why it has not. I think that sort of requirement in our committee system might be of considerable value.
I also suggest, in speaking of the committee system, that minority reports should be permitted to be tabled along with majority reports from committees. It seems to me that democracy not only means majority rule but also respect for minority opinions. It is simply not good enough to say that a member can always issue a press release or express his opinion in the House if he does not agree with a report which he has assisted in drawing up. Such ventures do not have equal weight with a formal, written document and tend to be transitory rather than part of the permanent record. If the education is a major role, or is of major importance, in the work of committees it would be valuable both to this House and to our population if minority opinions and reports were published in Votes and Proceedings along with majority opinions of committees.

subtopic: COMMITTEE REVIEW OF AND REPORT ON STANDING ORDERS AND PROCEDURE-AUTHORIZATION TO TRAVEL OUTSIDE OF CANADA DURING STUDY
speechtext:
I suggest that committees be granted a greater degree of independence from government control and that they be allowed an initiative in matters referred to them by the House. I have in mind that committees be allowed to present a resolution to the House suggesting a subject matter for committees to examine, rather than being forced to wait upon the government for action to be taken as is frequently the case. I think this procedure would overcome the argument that such initiatives on the part of committees would tend to obscure the fact that they are and should be subordinate to the House, because the House would determine the fate of the committee requests. The House can always turn down the request of a committee for a matter to be investigated.
May I make a few further very brief submissions about the organization of the committee system. I believe that the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization should look into the manner in which committee chairmen are selected and assigned. I think we should examine the possibility of adopting the British system in which committee chairmen are appointed either from the opposition or from the government. Also, I think we should examine the possibility of our having a panel of chairmen who might move from committee to committee. They would be members who are schooled in the rules. Committees might operate more effectively and efficiently under trained chairmen. Let us look at these ideas when examining our organization and procedure.
Leaving committees, I wish to say just a few words about the form in which legislation is presented to this House. In order to save time may I say, with respect to reasoned amendments, that I support the remarks by the hon. member for Peace River. More specifically, I wish to draw the attention of the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization to what seemed for a time to have become standard practice on the part of the government,
March 7, 1973

that of introducing omnibus bills, a practice about which Mr. Speaker has expressed great reservations on several occasions.
In order to illustrate my point and to show that this practice should be halted, may I refer to a bill introduced in the previous parliament, the government organization bill. When that bill was presented to the House we were asked, in considering it, to pass judgment on no less than nine different subject matters and on at least five, perhaps more, matters of principle with only one vote. The hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave), speaking in the second reading debate on that bill, summarized the situation as follows, as reported at page 2760 of Hansard for January 26, 1971:
To recapitulate in a slightly different way, we are being asked to create a new department; we are being asked to vary administrative duties of some existing departments; we are being asked to create ministers of the Crown who will formulate and develop government policy and, as well as providing for these salaried ministers, we are being asked to provide for additional salaried parliamentary secretaries. Distinct from those matters, we are also asked to vote yea or nay, without hearing witnesses, on behalf of those affected on the question of the retirement rights and obligations of public servants.
Steven Leacock once described this as a place where "men come together merely to hear the latest legislation and indulge in cheers, sighs, groans, votes and other expressions of vitality." I expect parliament often fits that description. But despite that, it serves the useful function of helping to focus public attention on matters of concern and of defining and delineating the considerations involved. In so doing, parliament aids the public in coming to intelligent conclusions about the actions of government and helps individual members of the public to decide their own position on questions of importance. This whole process, so key to the effective functioning of a democratic state, is injured and perhaps even dies when the issues before parliament become unfocused and blurred about the edges, as happens when the manner in which they are presented lacks clarity and precision. Nothing could obscure issues more than bringing before this House omnibus bills.
Under a majority government-I am not speaking of minority governments-with the well established pattern of voting solidly by party, votes in parliament are virtually meaningless and useless as a means of effecting parliamentary control. What is important in the functioning of parliament is that there be opportunity for discussions. What is important in the functioning of parliament is the quality of the discussion conducted. What is important in the functioning of parliament is that discussion be focused. How, in heaven's name, can discussion be focused when a bill includes as many as five different matters of principle? How are the gentlemen in the press gallery to follow the theme of a debate which may bounce from pollution, in the case of the government organization bill, to ministers' salaries, pensions, parliamentary secretaries, to the Post Office and back again? How, as a consequence, is the public supposed to form any opinion except that this House is in a hopeless mess.
These are some of the suggestions which I wish to present for the consideration of the House and, more specifically, to the members of the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. I hope that they will be
Standing Orders and Procedure
looked at closely. I have not said anything about supply procedures since I think most of the relevant considerations were mentioned by the two previous speakers. I shall finish now as I want to leave time for the representative of the Social Credit party to speak.

subtopic: COMMITTEE REVIEW OF AND REPORT ON STANDING ORDERS AND PROCEDURE-AUTHORIZATION TO TRAVEL OUTSIDE OF CANADA DURING STUDY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was eagerly waiting for the opportunity to take part in this debate on procedure and organization regarding the business of the House, in view of the fact that we are a third party but nevertheless belong here. Now, in most cases, Standing Orders which, as we know, were made several years ago, provide for only two parties, not four.
That is why consultations between House leaders have expanded in the last few years ago in order to make more flexible the two-party system, to enable the New Democratic Party, ours or any other to participate in the proceedings to a greater extent and to have their say in regulating the business of the House.
I am honoured to do this job which gives me the opportunity of finding a lot of small details in the Standing Orders-and sometimes important problems-which are such that our business is not always as efficient as you and we would wish.
Since this House represents the people of Canada, it must reflect in the course of its business what Canadians are expecting from us. They expect that the House business will have efficient results and enable hon. members to take a real part in the proceedings. The present provisions of the Standing Orders and the procedure being so complex, an hon. member who would like to represent his constituents adequately cannot always do so.
Given our minority government, one can see that the procedure has been more flexible and has let to better results. One can see as well that there has been at least twice as much consultation between parties as before. Therefore, I wonder why under a majority government and with the same Standing Orders we do not get the same results, there is less consultation and democracy in this House.
Does that mean that the procedure is here to serve the interests of one specific political party? Should the procedure not serve rather the interests of each hon. member at any time, regardless of the number of members in such or such party, and enable him to express himself, whether the government has a majority or not?
I will get the answer that because of the interests of the people there is obviously a need because of the minority government for further discussions, further consultations, further consideration of the views of all hon. members. I would say to that that it is abnormal for a minority government to serve the interest of the people better than a majority government. I think that both should serve the people equally since it is the express wish of the people to elect either a majority or minority government. This is why in both cases the people should have a right to expect efficiency on the part of hon. members.
Mr. Speaker, my general remarks address themselves to the motion introduced today by the President of the Privy

March 7, 1973
Standing Orders and Procedure Council (Mr. MacEachen) to refer to the Committee on Procedure and Organization the 60 or 80 recommendations that you yourself suggested very cleverly during the two last Parliaments and to also have a study made of the various criticisms that hon. members had to make on the subject of procedure so as to make it more contemporary and efficient. That is why I support this motion which will enable us to improve procedure.
I think that the motion currently before the House provides the Committee on Procedure and Organization with broad enough terms of reference so that there is enough reason to hope for a thorough reform of our Standing Orders as well as the procedure of the House and its committees; at more or less regular intervals the House of Commons usually revises its rules and procedures to make them more efficient and accelerate its proceedings and debates.
Several hon. members complain-rightly I am sure- about several aspects of parliamentary business. The major problem is undoubtedly the question period which has become a real cause of frustration for most hon. members as well as the Chair.
When I say it is frustrating for most hon. members, I am not referring to front benchers, but to the very great majority of back benchers, if not all, whose only hope lies in the notorious supplementary question. If hon. members could not fall back on supplementary questions and if they were ruled out on a trial basis, let's say for a week, keeping to the same system, it would be seen that front benchers, willing or unwilling, would then have to give back benchers a chance to put questions.
In my opinion, the Chair's problem, and ours, stems from abusive recourse to supplementary questions, and I shall return to that later.
The second problem I should like to bring to the attention to my colleagues is conflicting schedules. When standing committees and the House are in session simultaneously, an hon. member should be in the House, where he is in duty bound to be, and also in a parliamentary committee to which he has been duly convened. Since he is not gifted with ubiquity, this leads to vast problems for hon. members. I understand that discussions are under way between various parties in the House to establish a fair schedule allowing efficient functioning of both the House and the committees. However, Mr. Speaker, I doubt whether anything can be achieved by juggling schedules. I rather believe our schedules should indicate periods for committee work and periods for the proceedings of the House of Commons.
There is a third problem that I should like to bring to the attention of the House: it is the ridiculousness of setting aside an hour for private members to introduce bills or motions for papers when there is little or no chance of their proposals' receiving serious consideration.
As all hon. members know, at the beginning of the session, as long as the first 40 hours have not been taken up, an hour is set aside on Mondays, Tuesdays, Thursdays and Fridays for private members' business, while if the 40 hours have been used up, only two hours are set aside for that purpose.
[Mr. Fortin.l
On the other hand, it is clear from the items on the Order Paper that the volume of private members' business is increasing all the time; a way out of this situation will have to be found, not only so as to encourage private members to introduce bills or motions, but also so as to afford them some hope of getting them heard.
For my part, I have been proposing the same motion for five years, since I came to the House. The motion was finally debated in the fifth year, which is perfectly ridiculous, and shows once again that some members are justly frustrated by the excuse that they do not sit on the government benches. This is a blatant contradiction of the professions of democracy that are broadcast during election campaigns so as to win votes.
My fourth point is that when specific motions are introduced under Standing Order 43, requiring the unanimous consent of the House, they can be rejected by any member, without his identity having to be revealed.
According to Standing Order 26, if an hon. member raises a question of national emergency after giving notice to the Speaker, what happens? The Speaker then decides for himself whether the motion is of national urgency or not. In fact, the Speaker alone is responsible for deciding whether the motion is in order under Standing Order 26.
Therefore, I cannot see how it would be fair to allow hon. members to say "no" in an anonymous way, without anybody knowing who they are. Frankly, I think that, if the Speaker is called upon to decide whether a motion proposed under Standing Order 26 is in order, a member opposing a motion under Standing Order 43 should identify himself. I am sure nobody is going to agree with my proposal.
Mr. Speaker, this shows how ridiculous Standing Order 43 is. This rule has become for most members the only possibility to speak on a particular and important problem by way of a motion. Anyway, a solution will have to be found to the problem arising from Standing Order 43 because I am convinced that it will continue to bother the Chair, to delay the question period and yet to satisfy hon. members resorting to it since, otherwise, they would not be able to participate in the oral question period. And all this is due to Standing Orders 43 being abused.
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to deal with the problem of committee business which has taken ever more significance, specially since 1970. In fact, since then the number of questions referred to the committees for study has been increasing. Consequently, the committee business has been slowing down, the agenda is so overloaded that sometimes we are completely confused. It has become extremely hard work and it should not be forgotten that the committees' working hours are in conflict with the House sittings. The committees' workload has grown heavier for the last few years. This was not bad as an experience but I also think that any procedure reform is somewhat experimental. Consequently, I wonder whether it would not be desirable that the committees seriously study the possibility of increasing the workload of the committee of the whole House instead of handling more work themselves. I do not mean that all questions should be referred to the committee of the whole House but surely it would be desirable that, when introducing its
March 7, 1973

bills, the government should decide which legislation will be studied in committee of the whole House. We should also study the possibility of using more the committee of the whole House which enables hon. members to work all the more meaningfully as they work publicly. In fact, they can discuss with ministers and with quite a few hon. members and this permits them to get information on questions with which they are not so familiar. Therefore, this is surely a thing which, to my mind, should be considered.
I would like now to talk briefly about the problem of written questions. I shall make but one remark on this, to say that the time it takes the government to answer questions on the order paper makes us wonder whether this has not become a practice or policy.
The questions on the Order Paper deal with extremely serious matters, Mr. Speaker. Under Standing Order 39- if I remember correctly-a practice has been strongly established thanks to the ability of the Chair, namely that when a member puts a question orally and that, in the opinion of Mr. Speaker, it is not obviously urgent, he may suggest to the member that the question be put on the Order Paper. Three months later, the member is still waiting for an answer. This is why, Mr. Speaker, delays in answering questions on the order paper are annoying the member and put him in a difficult position.
On the one hand, we do not want to challenge the Speaker's ruling-and I think that this is a good thing- and on the other hand, we must agree, at his request, to put the question on the Order Paper. Furthermore, there is no way we can demand a written answer to our question from the government. Consequently, I think that this is a serious shortcoming of Standing Orders and constitutes an interference with the member's right and privilege to obtain information as he is entitled to.
I will make the same remark about motions for papers. That matter has been raised today on a point of order. I refrained from making any comment in that connection, because I felt it would delay the proceedings and that the matter was being raised at the wrong time. Since it is now the right time, I will merely say, as far as motions for papers are concerned, that some 20 per cent are acceptable to the government and that at least 80 per cent are rejected. The very clever Standing Orders governing our proceedings-if you will allow me to say so, Mr. Speaker- then provides that such a matter may be transferred for debate. Now, when will the matter be discussed? Never! When two Sundays come in one week! Thus the member is frustrated and denied the right and privilege of obtaining some papers or specific statistics. The hon. member has no other choice but to write to the minister but even then, what with bureaucracy, he never sees the end of it.
That is why, I am anxious for the President of the Privy Council to reveal on the basis of what criteria motions for papers are accepted or rejected, that we might be able to judge whether they are truly honest, fair and equitable, and whether they, in fact, respect the rights and privileges of hon. members.
Mr. Speaker, I will come back to oral questions and to Standing Order 39(5). Since 1964, hon. members have had the privilege of being asked to put their questions on the Order Paper when their urgency is not obvious or when
Standing Orders and Procedure
they call for statistical data. That, to my mind, is an excellent rule, because it allows some control of the quality of the questions. In fact, if a question is not a matter of urgent public interest, it surely does not belong in the oral question period. I think this is an excellent practice.
However, I wonder why there should not be some kind of control or co-ordination on the subject of supplementary questions. I have discussed the matter of the oral question period with my Creditiste colleagues. This is one aspect we are surely going to delve into from beginning to end and we are not going to quit because this has become a highly ridiculous situation. To realize this, one only has to sit in the gallery and ask the people what they think of the oral question period.
When people leave this place, Mr. Speaker-and hon. members will forgive the expression because we are in a place where we faithfully express the views of our constituents-they think very often that it is a circus.
Mr. Speaker, I think that our fellow citizens who watch the question period are right. We suggest that we now have enough time, but that we make bad use of it. We make bad use of the 40 minutes. If we extend it to 80 minutes without changing the rules, we will not improve the situation.
It seems to me that the 40 minute period is long enough. However, there should be a fair division of time between opposition parties during the oral question period. There should be a first round with a maximum of two supplementary questions and then we could come back to allow more hon. members to participate in the question period.
There is nothing preventing us from coming back on the subject a second time.
We also discussed other subjects in this House-
